Disorder-induced proximate quantum spin ice phase in Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}

Abstract

Magnetic pyrochlores with non-Kramers rare-earth ions provide a platform for exploring emergent gauge physics and quantum spin-ice behavior, yet the influence of structural disorder on their ground states remains insufficiently understood. Here we combine bulk characterization and single-crystal neutron-scattering measurements to investigate the non-Kramers pyrochlore Pr2Sn2O7. At temperatures below ∼1\sim 1 K, the system exhibits key hallmarks of quantum spin-ice physics, including anisotropic spin-ice correlations and two distinct dynamical timescales. Upon further cooling, however, we observe a complete spin-freezing transition at Tf≈0.15T_{f}\approx 0.15 K, accompanied by recovery of the full nuclear Schottky anomaly, the emergence of a gapped magnetic excitation, and the development of incipient (100)(100) magnetic correlations. Comparison with related Pr-based pyrochlores places Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} near the spin-frozen boundary of a disorder-perturbed phase diagram. These results establish a disorder-driven framework for the evolution of quantum spin-ice behavior into frozen ground states, revealing how signatures of a proximate quantum spin liquid can persist despite disorder-induced spin freezing in non-Kramers pyrochlores.

I Introduction

The discovery of classical spin ice (CSI) phases in rare-earth pyrochlores [14, 17] represents a key milestone in frustrated magnetism, with potential implications for quantum information and magnetic storage [10, 60]. In these systems, strong Ising anisotropy and effective ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor interactions stabilize a “two-in, two-out” ground state, with magnetic moments aligned along local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle directions. This configuration gives rise to an extensively degenerate manifold [41] and dipolar spin correlations that manifest as pinch-point features in neutron scattering [17]. The inclusion of transverse exchange interactions introduces quantum fluctuations, leading to quantum spin ice (QSI), in which tunneling between ice-rule configurations stabilizes a U⁡(1)U(1) quantum spin liquid (QSL) [25, 46]. Beyond spinon excitations inherited from CSI, the QSI phase supports emergent gauge excitations, including gapless photon-like modes and gapped topological defects (visons, or “magnetic monopoles”) [22, 11, 12]. Early discussions of QSI focused on materials such as Yb2​Ti2​O7\text{Yb}_{2}\text{Ti}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [44, 48, 42]. More recently, Ce-based pyrochlores, such as Ce2​Zr2​O7\text{Ce}_{2}\text{Zr}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [21, 7, 19, 52, 54, 20], Ce2​Sn2​O7\text{Ce}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [49, 39, 59], and Ce2​Hf2​O7\text{Ce}_{2}\text{Hf}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [38, 53], have emerged as particularly promising platforms for realizing quantum spin-liquid physics.

Pr-based pyrochlores constitute another family of promising QSI candidates, featuring a non-Kramers ground-state doublet well separated from the first excited crystal-field (CF) level (≳10\gtrsim 10 meV) [28, 3, 40]. Their low-temperature properties are thus governed by an effective pseudospin-1/21/2 degree of freedom on each Pr3+ site. The symmetry-allowed Hamiltonian in the local coordinate frame takes the form

ℋ=∑⟨i​j⟩,nJnσizσjz+∑⟨i​j⟩,1{−J±(σ+iσ−j+σ−iσ+j)+J±⁣±[γi​jσ+iσ+j+γi​j∗σ−iσ−j]}−∑ihiσix,\begin{split}\mathcal{H}&=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,n}J_{n}\sigma_{i}^{z}\sigma_{j}^{z}+\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,1}\left\{-J_{\pm}(\sigma^{+}_{i}\sigma^{-}_{j}+\sigma^{-}_{i}\sigma^{+}_{j})\right.\\ &\left.+J_{\pm\pm}\left[\gamma_{ij}\sigma^{+}_{i}\sigma^{+}_{j}+\gamma_{ij}^{*}\sigma^{-}_{i}\sigma^{-}_{j}\right]\right\}-\sum_{i}h_{i}\sigma_{i}^{x},\end{split} (1)

Here, σix,y,z\sigma_{i}^{x,y,z} are Pauli matrices. The component σiz\sigma_{i}^{z} denotes the longitudinal dipole moment along ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle, and nearest-neighbor Ising interactions J1>0J_{1}>0 stabilize the “two-in, two-out” state, while further-neighbor longitudinal couplings (n>1n>1) are included for completeness. The transverse components σix,y\sigma_{i}^{x,y} (with σi±≡σix±i​σiy\sigma_{i}^{\pm}\equiv\sigma_{i}^{x}\pm i\sigma_{i}^{y}) correspond to quadrupolar degrees of freedom [40, 37], while symmetry-allowed nearest-neighbor transverse interactions J±J_{\pm} and J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} introduce quantum fluctuations [44, 37]. In real Pr-based systems, the non-Kramers ground-state doublet can be split by perturbations or disorder that break the local D3​dD_{3d} symmetry. This effect is captured by a site-dependent transverse field hih_{i} coupled to the quadrupolar component σix\sigma_{i}^{x} [58, 31, 6, 15][Fig. 1(a)].

In the perturbative limit of the nearest-neighbor model, where |J±|,|hi|≪J1|J_{\pm}|,|h_{i}|\ll J_{1} and J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} is neglected as a subleading term, the low-energy dynamics is governed by an effective ring-exchange process [Fig. 1(b)],

ℋring=−∑⎔(KJ+Ki​j​k​l​m​nh)σi+σj−σk+σl−σm+σn−+H.c.,\mathcal{H}_{\text{ring}}=-\sum_{\hexagon}\left(K^{J}+K^{h}_{ijklmn}\right)\sigma^{+}_{i}\sigma^{-}_{j}\sigma^{+}_{k}\sigma^{-}_{l}\sigma^{+}_{m}\sigma^{-}_{n}+\text{H.c.}, (2)

stabilizing a non-Kramers QSI phase. The uniform contribution KJ=12​J±3/J12K^{J}=12J_{\pm}^{3}/J_{1}^{2} arises from transverse exchange [25, 5], while the plaquette-dependent term Ki​j​k​l​m​nh=63​hi​hj​hk​hl​hm​hn/16​J15K^{h}_{ijklmn}=63\,h_{i}h_{j}h_{k}h_{l}h_{m}h_{n}/16J_{1}^{5} originates from site-dependent transverse fields [47, 6].

In the non-Kramers QSI regime, the neutron-scattering response is theoretically predicted to be dominated by photon-like excitations, with a vanishing spinon contribution [12, 2], in contrast to experimental observations in Pr-based QSI candidates. In Pr2​Zr2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Zr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}, more than 90% of the spectral weight resides in a broad inelastic continuum [28, 37], later attributed to disorder-induced transverse fields and transitions within split ground-state doublets [58, 31]. By comparison, Pr2​Hf2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Hf}_{2}\text{O}_{7} displays enhanced quasielastic spectral weight and a reduced inelastic response forming a gapped excitation near ℏ​ω≈0.2\hbar\omega\approx 0.2 meV [51, 50]. In both compounds, the inelastic magnetic scattering displays a characteristic “star-fish-like” [58] 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence devoid of pinch-point features. Furthermore, pronounced sample dependence observed in low-temperature heat capacity and susceptibility for Pr2​Zr2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Zr}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [28, 55], Pr2​Hf2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Hf}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [51, 3], and Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [32, 33], points to a dominant role of disorder over intrinsic transverse interactions.

Although a complete theoretical framework for disordered QSIs remains lacking, the experimental observations above motivate a useful conceptual phase diagram [Fig. 1(c)], constructed by extending models originally developed for disordered nearest-neighbor CSI systems [47, 6, 35]. This description is formulated in the limit |J±|≪J1|J_{\pm}|\ll J_{1}, with J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} neglected, while allowing for finite, spatially varying hih_{i} that governs the phase behavior together with J1>0J_{1}>0. Within this framework, h¯\bar{h} denotes the spatial average of hih_{i}, while δ​h\delta h characterizes the width of its distribution, without assuming a specific functional form.

Within this phase diagram, a QSI state is stabilized for weak and nearly uniform hih_{i}, while two instabilities can drive the system out of this regime [6]. First, for a nearly uniform transverse field with h¯≳hc≈0.6​J1\bar{h}\gtrsim h_{c}\approx 0.6J_{1}, spinons condense, leading to a paramagnetic state composed of site-localized singlets [43, 6]. Second, when the width of the disorder distribution exceeds a critical threshold, δ​h>δ​hc\delta h>\delta h_{c}, spatial inhomogeneity in the ring-exchange amplitudes [Eq. 2] localizes quantum tunneling to plaquettes proximate to disorder and promotes the local proliferation of visons in these regions [47, 6]. This favors Ising ordering with a (100)(100) propagation vector [11]; however, long-range order is suppressed by disorder, resulting instead in a spin-frozen state with frozen magnetic moments [6]. For QSI candidates, the critical disorder variance at vanishing average field, δ​hc\delta h_{c}, is expected to remain finite due to quantum fluctuations arising from intrinsic transverse interactions. For finite δ​h\delta h [24, 47], Griffiths-type regimes may also emerge, in which rare regions locally satisfy h¯>hc\bar{h}>h_{c} and behave paramagnetically, while the bulk remains either fluctuating (a “Griffiths QSI” regime) or frozen (a “Griffiths spin-frozen” regime).

A central challenge in realizing quantum spin liquids in real materials is understanding how weak disorder reshapes their emergent excitations and ground states, and drives systems into proximate phases within a disorder-influenced phase diagram. Among the Pr-based pyrochlores, Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} has long been considered a promising QSI candidate, hosting a non-Kramers ground-state doublet for Pr3+ that is well separated from higher crystal-field levels [40]. Spins remain dynamically fluctuating down to at least 0.2 K without signatures of long-range order, as evidenced by low-energy magnetic scattering extending to ∼0.2\sim 0.2 meV [62, 33].

In this work, we present the first comprehensive experimental study of flux-grown single-crystal Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}, combining neutron scattering with bulk thermodynamic measurements. We show that, at intermediate temperatures below ∼1\sim 1 K, the system exhibits clear signatures of quantum spin-ice behavior, including anisotropic spin-ice correlations and two well-separated dynamical timescales consistent with theoretical expectations and prior powder studies. Upon further cooling, the system undergoes a disorder-induced spin-freezing transition below Tf≈0.15T_{f}\approx 0.15 K, accompanied by a persistent gapped magnetic excitation and incipient (100)(100) correlations. These results place flux-grown Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} near the fully spin-frozen boundary in close proximity to the QSI phase and, when considered alongside prior studies, suggest a unified disorder-driven framework for interpreting the diverse behavior across Pr-based pyrochlores, with phenomenology reminiscent of Griffiths-type regimes.

II Results

II.1 Equal-time magnetic correlations

Single-crystal magnetic diffuse scattering measured at T=0.3T=0.3 K and T=1T=1 K is shown in Fig. 2a and Fig. 2e, respectively. At T=1T=1 K [Fig. 2e], Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} already exhibits a characteristic pinch-point–like pattern, signaling the onset of spin-ice correlations. Upon cooling to T=0.3T=0.3 K [Fig. 2a], the scattering develops a more anisotropic and asymmetric structure. Compared with simulations of the classical nearest-neighbor spin-ice (NNSI) model [5] [Fig. 2c], the experimental data display enhanced anisotropy along the [001][001] and [111][111] directions and broader intensity near the (222)(222) position, indicating that the T=0.3T=0.3 K data cannot be adequately described by the NNSI model alone.

To elucidate the origin of the observed 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence, we analyze the data using two complementary theoretical descriptions. First, we consider the QSI model of Ref. [5], characterized by a uniform ring-exchange interaction Keff≡KJ+K¯hK^{\mathrm{eff}}\equiv K^{J}+\bar{K}^{h} [Eq. 2], where K¯h\bar{K}^{h} is taken as the average of Ki​j​k​l​m​nhK^{h}_{ijklmn} over all hexagonal plaquettes. The best fit yields Keff=0.0065​(3)K^{\mathrm{eff}}=0.0065(3) meV. Second, we employ a classical dipolar spin-ice (DSI) model [34], incorporating calculated dipolar interactions Ddip≈0.0010D_{\mathrm{dip}}\approx 0.0010 meV. Within this framework, the nnth-neighbor coupling is given by Jn=Jnex+DnJ_{n}=J_{n}^{\mathrm{ex}}+D_{n}, where JnexJ_{n}^{\mathrm{ex}} denotes the exchange contribution and DnD_{n} the effective dipolar term (see Sec.S3 of the Supplementary Materials for details). Satisfactory agreement requires exchange interactions beyond nearest neighbors, and can be achieved with J1ex=0.0215​(26)J_{1}^{\mathrm{ex}}=0.0215(26) meV and second-neighbor exchange J2ex=−0.0016​(1)J_{2}^{\mathrm{ex}}=-0.0016(1) meV. Notably, both the QSI model [Fig. 2b,f] and the extended DSI model [Fig. 2d,h] provide excellent descriptions of the measured scattering.

On the basis of equal-time correlations alone, it is therefore not possible to disentangle the roles of quantum dynamics and further-neighbor interactions. To resolve this ambiguity, we turn to the theoretical prediction that a QSI phase in Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} should exhibit two well-separated dynamical timescales [56]: a slow component, τslow\tau_{\mathrm{slow}}, accessible via a.c. susceptibility, and a fast component, τfast\tau_{\mathrm{fast}}, probed by inelastic neutron scattering. We therefore employ both techniques to investigate the spin dynamics.

II.2 A.c. susceptibility

As shown in Fig. 3a,b, zero-field a.c. susceptibility measurements on single-crystal Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} reveal a progressive slowing of spin dynamics upon cooling below ∼1\sim 1 K. This is evidenced by the pronounced frequency dependence of the real component, χ′\chi^{\prime}, whose peak shifts to higher temperatures with increasing measurement frequency. Upon further cooling, the system undergoes a spin-freezing transition at Tf≈0.15T_{f}\approx 0.15 K, below which χ′\chi^{\prime} is strongly suppressed and approaches zero. Consistently, the imaginary component χ′′\chi^{\prime\prime} exhibits a clear peak at temperatures above TfT_{f} for all measured frequencies, indicative of dissipative spin dynamics preceding the frozen state [57].

Fitting χ′\chi^{\prime} using a damped harmonic oscillator model [Eq. 3] [57, 33] yields a slow relaxation timescale τslow\tau_{\mathrm{slow}} spanning approximately 10−610^{-6}–10−210^{-2} s below 1 K, with a characteristic value τslow∼10−5\tau_{\mathrm{slow}}\sim 10^{-5}-10−410^{-4} s just above the freezing transition [Fig. 3i]. The frequency dependence of TfT_{f}, determined from the peak position in χ′′\chi^{\prime\prime} [Fig. 3b], is well described by Arrhenius behavior, f=f0​exp(−Ea/kBTf)f=f_{0}\exp(-E_a/k_{\mathrm{B}}T_f), with an activation energy Ea=0.23​(6)E_{a}=0.23(6) meV and an attempt frequency f0≈80f_{0}\approx 80 MHz, where f0f_{0} should be regarded as an order-of-magnitude estimate [Fig. 3c], in good agreement with previous results on powder samples [33].

II.3 Nuclear Schottky anomaly

The spin-freezing transition is further reflected in the zero-field heat capacity, CpC_{p} [Fig. 3d], which displays a pronounced nuclear Schottky anomaly approaching the theoretical maximum value of ∼7​J/(molPr3+​K)\sim 7\penalty\ \mathrm{J}/(\mathrm{mol}_{\mathrm{Pr^{3+}}}\,\mathrm{K}) at base temperature. This behavior is consistent with fully frozen Pr moments below TfT_{f} [28, 55]. After subtracting the hyperfine contribution [28, 23], the magnetic entropy released between the base temperature (∼0.1\sim 0.1 K) and 10 K is found to be comparable to the Pauling value R⁡(ln⁡2−12​ln⁡32)R\!\left(\ln 2-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\tfrac{3}{2}\right) [Fig. 3ii]. Although a definitive separation of the nuclear and electronic contributions to the heat capacity is not possible, this result is broadly consistent with the expectation that most spin-ice entropy is released below 10 K and that spin-ice correlations are largely absent at 10 K.

II.4 Elastic and inelastic neutron scattering

Neutron spectroscopy provides key insight into spin dynamics both above and below TfT_{f}. The energy dependence of the powder-averaged scattering is shown in Fig. 4a–c. At T=10T=10 K, pronounced inelastic scattering extends up to 0.60.6 meV [Fig. 4c], which we attribute to transitions between the two singlets of the non-Kramers ground-state doublet split by site-dependent transverse fields hih_{i} [58, 31]. These transitions are hereafter referred to as the singlet–singlet excitation. The spectra are well described by a model of independent singlet–singlet excitations with energy transfer Δi=2​hi\Delta_{i}=2h_{i} [Eq. 10], assuming a half-Lorentzian distribution of hih_{i} [Eq. 11]. The corresponding fit is shown as a dashed line in Fig. 4c. The extracted half-width at half-maximum (HWHM) of the inelastic scattering is ΓΔ=2​Γh=0.13​(1)\Gamma_{\Delta}=2\Gamma_{h}=0.13(1) meV, where Γh=0.063​(3)\Gamma_{h}=0.063(3) meV is significantly smaller than the value Γh=0.27​(1)\Gamma_{h}=0.27(1) meV reported for floating-zone–grown Pr2​Zr2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Zr}_{2}\text{O}_{7} samples [58].

Upon cooling below T∼1T\sim 1 K, spin-ice correlations progressively develop in Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}, leading to a pronounced evolution of the singlet–singlet excitation. The excitation shifts to higher energies, accompanied by a redistribution of spectral weight from the inelastic channel toward the quasielastic channel, where signatures of QSI physics may emerge. A mean-field description of this evolution is provided in Methods. At T=0.5T=0.5 K, both modified singlet–singlet excitations and finite-temperature QSI excitations are expected to contribute; however, these components cannot be resolved separately at the present experimental resolution. To phenomenologically describe the spectra, we model the response using a damped harmonic oscillator (DHO) form [Eq. 14], which yields overdamped dynamics with characteristic timescales on the order of τ∼10−11\tau\sim 10^{-11} s, comparable to the fast relaxation channel τfast\tau_{\mathrm{fast}} identified in Ref. [56]. Because a substantial fraction of the inelastic response originates from overlapping singlet–singlet excitations, the extracted timescale should be regarded as a lower bound on the intrinsic QSI relaxation time. The remaining low-energy spectral weight near zero energy transfer may arise from photon-like QSI excitations that remain unresolved from the elastic line.

At T=0.05T=0.05 K, well below TfT_{f}, the magnetic excitation spectrum undergoes a pronounced transformation. Relative to T=0.5T=0.5 K, the low-energy inelastic spectral weight in the range [0, 0.2][0,\,0.2] meV is strongly suppressed, while a well-defined gapped excitation persists. As QSI dynamics are expected to be suppressed below the spin-freezing transition, the inelastic response in this regime is attributed entirely to the modified singlet–singlet excitation. Analysis using the DHO form [Eq. 14] yields a damped propagating mode centered at Egap=0.23​(1)E_{\mathrm{gap}}=0.23(1) meV with a HWHM Γ=0.12​(2)\Gamma=0.12(2) meV. The gap energy is in good agreement with the activation energy Ea=0.23​(6)E_{a}=0.23(6) meV extracted from a.c. susceptibility measurements. The linewidth Γ\Gamma is comparable to ΓΔ\Gamma_{\Delta} at T=10T=10 K, indicating that the broadening is similarly governed by the distribution of quenched disorder.

By integrating the fitted dynamical response functions (dashed lines in Fig. 4a–c), we find that the integrated intensity at T=0.05T=0.05 K and T=0.5T=0.5 K accounts for approximately 30%30\% and 80%80\%, respectively, of the total fitted magnetic spectral weight observed at T=10T=10 K, denoted as I0I_{0}. Consistent with the total-moment sum rule, the spectral weight lost upon cooling is transferred to energies within the elastic resolution.

Two mechanisms likely contribute to the redistribution of spectral weight across the spin-freezing transition at TfT_{f}. First, the evolution from T=0.5T=0.5 K to T=0.05T=0.05 K qualitatively follows the expected temperature dependence of the singlet–singlet excitation as spin-ice correlations develop. However, this effect alone is unlikely to account for the full ∼50%​I0\sim 50\%\,I_{0} transfer of spectral weight from the dynamical channel into the elastic channel, since spin-ice correlations are already well developed at T=0.5T=0.5 K [Fig. 4d], and a substantial further enhancement of the exchange field at lower temperatures is not expected.

A second contribution arises from the suppression of QSI-related excitations present above TfT_{f} upon entering the frozen state. In Pr-based QSI candidates, spin freezing has been theoretically predicted to favor (100)(100) magnetic order through vison condensation [11, 6], consistent with the incipient (100)(100) correlations observed here (see below). A quantitative separation of these two contributions would require higher energy and temperature resolution than available in the present study.

We next examine the 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence of the magnetic scattering, shown in Fig. 4d–j for T=0.05T=0.05 K and T=0.5T=0.5 K at representative energy ranges. These constant-energy slices are intended to highlight the momentum dependence of the magnetic scattering after background subtraction; quantitative comparisons of absolute intensity between panels are not meaningful (see Methods). At T=0.5T=0.5 K, the elastic scattering [Fig. 4d] exhibits a pinch-point–like pattern, consistent with spin-ice correlations. Upon further cooling into the spin-frozen state at T=0.05T=0.05 K, the elastic scattering evolves markedly [Fig. 4e], with intensity concentrated near reciprocal-space positions including (001)(001), (003)(003), (110)(110), (1±2 0)(1\pm 2\,0), and (2±1 0)(2\pm 1\,0). This redistribution suggests the development of short-range correlations with an incipient ordering wavevector 𝒒=(100)\bm{q}=(100) as the system freezes.

Similar tendencies have been reported in classical spin-ice (CSI) materials Ho2​Ti2​O7\text{Ho}_{2}\text{Ti}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [9, 27] and Dy2​Ti2​O7\text{Dy}_{2}\text{Ti}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [61, 45] below their respective freezing temperatures. In those systems, however, deviations from ideal pinch-point behavior are weaker, and the freezing is commonly attributed to stronger dipolar interactions acting alongside geometric frustration [45]. By contrast, within the QSI framework, spin freezing of the magnetic dipole component corresponds to a confinement transition of the emergent U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field, which generically breaks translational symmetry. The simplest ordering tendency emerging from this theoretical framework is characterized by a propagation vector 𝒒=(100)\bm{q}=(100) [11, 6], qualitatively consistent with the diffuse scattering observed here.

The 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence of the gapped excitation at T=0.05T=0.05 K [Fig. 4a] over the energy range |ℏ​ω|∈[0.2, 0.6]|\hbar\omega|\in[0.2,\,0.6] meV [Fig. 4g] exhibits a characteristic “star-fish-like” pattern. A similar, albeit more diffuse, structure is observed at T=0.5T=0.5 K [Fig. 4f] in the same energy range. By contrast, at higher energy transfers ℏ​ω≳0.6\hbar\omega\gtrsim 0.6 meV [Fig. 4h,j], no significant 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence is resolved within the experimental sensitivity. These observations are consistent with singlet–singlet excitations modified by spin-ice correlations [58, 6], and closely resemble inelastic magnetic features reported in Pr2​Zr2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Zr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}[28, 37, 58] and Pr2​Hf2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Hf}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [50]. The contrasting 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence of the elastic and inelastic channels at T=0.5T=0.5 K further demonstrates that spin-ice correlations are well developed despite the presence of disorder-induced inelastic scattering.

II.5 Characterization of structural disorder

Our bulk measurements and neutron spectroscopy together indicate the presence of disorder in Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}, motivating a detailed examination of its structural origin. To this end, powder neutron diffraction measurements were performed on pulverized single-crystal material, and several candidate disorder models were tested via Rietveld refinement. These included: (i) partial oxidation of Pr, corresponding to Pr2Sn2O7+y with Pr4+ occupying the Pr site; (ii) antisite cation disorder, in which Pr partially occupies the Sn site, modeled as Pr2(Sn2-xPrx)O7+y; and (iii) Frenkel-type oxygen disorder, involving displacement of oxygen atoms to the interstitial (18,18,18)(\tfrac{1}{8},\,\tfrac{1}{8},\,\tfrac{1}{8}) position of the cubic unit cell. In all cases, the best agreement with the diffraction data was obtained for models without resolvable disorder [Fig. 5a,b], placing an upper bound of ≲1%\lesssim 1\% on the concentration of each disorder type considered. Consistently, no evidence for significant ionic off-centering was found, as the refined anisotropic atomic displacement parameters remain within typical values [Table S1].

To probe disorder beyond the sensitivity of average-structure refinement, we performed neutron pair-distribution-function (PDF) analysis [Fig. 5c], which provides a complementary real-space perspective. Refinement of the Fd3¯\bar{3}m pyrochlore structure using symmetry-allowed anisotropic atomic displacement parameters (ADPs) yields a significantly improved overall agreement with the data (Rw=7.71%R_{w}=7.71\%) compared with an isotropic model (Rw=9.33%R_{w}=9.33\%). The incorporation of anisotropic ADPs notably improves the description of the Pr–O and O–O correlations at interatomic distances of 2.587 Å and 2.727 Å, respectively, while slightly degrading the description of the nearest-neighbor metal–metal correlation at 3.746 Å. These results indicate that the local disorder is predominantly accommodated through displacements of the oxygen sublattice, producing subtle distortions of the PrO8 and/or SnO6 coordination polyhedra while largely preserving the metal-ion positions defined by the average crystal structure. Together, these results demonstrate that disorder in Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} is weak and predominantly local, remaining essentially undetectable by conventional Rietveld refinement, yet still capable of strongly influencing the ultra-low-temperature magnetic behavior because of the non-Kramers nature of the system. In addition, the refined lattice parameter exhibits a weak dependence on the maximum real-space fitting range (10–20 Å), consistent with the presence of local strains in the sample. The best-fit PDF refinement using anisotropic ADPs is shown in Fig. 5c, while the refined structural parameters from both the Rietveld and PDF refinements are summarized in Table S1 of the Supplementary Materials.

III Discussion

The convergence of multiple independent experimental probes demonstrates that our Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} samples exhibit magnetic properties broadly consistent with a QSI regime at finite temperatures below ∼1\sim 1 K. These include pronounced anisotropic spin-ice correlations together with two well-separated dynamical timescales, τslow∼10−5\tau_{\mathrm{slow}}\sim 10^{-5}-10−410^{-4} s and τfast∼10−11\tau_{\mathrm{fast}}\sim 10^{-11} s, indicative of a bimodal distribution of magnetic dynamics associated with local spin-flip processes [56]. Upon further cooling, however, the system undergoes a complete spin-freezing transition at Tf≈0.15T_{f}\approx 0.15 K, signaling a clear departure from QSI behavior and the emergence of a distinct low-temperature phase as T→0T\rightarrow 0.

This departure is most naturally attributed to weak structural disorder. Such an interpretation is supported by the pronounced sample dependence of ultra–low-temperature magnetic behavior reported for nominally identical compounds prepared via different synthesis routes. Although a quantitative characterization of disorder in Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} is beyond the scope of the present work, and the microscopic origin of disorder may vary across Pr-based pyrochlores [29, 31, 50, 26], its impact on low-temperature magnetism can be understood within a unified framework based on Eq. 1 and the conceptual phase diagram shown in Fig. 1c. To place our results within this framework, we compare Γh=0.063​(3)\Gamma_{h}=0.063(3) meV (as a proxy for h¯\bar{h}) with J1=J1ex+D1≈0.033J_{1}=J_{1}^{\mathrm{ex}}+D_{1}\approx 0.033 meV from the DSI analysis of magnetic diffuse scattering. These comparable energy scales (h¯/J1∼𝒪⁡(1)\bar{h}/J_{1}\sim\mathcal{O}(1)) place our system near the regime where uniform-field theory [43, 6] predicts an instability of the QSI phase at hc≈0.6​J1h_{c}\approx 0.6J_{1}, highlighting the role of transverse fields in destabilizing QSI behavior.

In this regime, both disorder-induced states proximate to the QSI phase are relevant for interpreting our results. The first is a paramagnetic regime, characterized by a broad inelastic continuum of singlet–singlet excitations that remains dominant down to base temperature, despite a partial reduction of spectral weight associated with the development of spin-ice correlations, which also impart a “star-fish-like” 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence to the excitations [58, 31, 6]. The second is a spin-frozen regime, signaled by slow dynamics in a.c. susceptibility, the emergence of a nuclear Schottky anomaly in low-temperature heat capacity, and incipient magnetic correlations consistent with vison condensation [11].

A comparison of these experimental diagnostics across representative Pr-based pyrochlores is summarized in Table 1. Within the framework of disorder-perturbed non-Kramers systems, these two instabilities are not expected to be mutually exclusive. Instead, the phenomenology exhibited by the materials listed in Table 1 is broadly consistent with a Griffiths-type spin-frozen framework, interpolating between paramagnetic and frozen limits in which signatures of both may coexist. Here, we use “Griffiths spin-frozen state” in a phenomenological sense to describe such coexistence, without requiring spatially rare paramagnetic regions in the strict microscopic sense [24].

Single-crystal Pr2​Zr2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Zr}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [28] and powder Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [33] exhibit behavior that lies closer to the paramagnetic side of this regime. In both cases, the nuclear Schottky anomaly is substantially reduced from its theoretical maximum of ∼7​J/(molPr3+​K)\sim 7\penalty\ \mathrm{J}/(\mathrm{mol}_{\mathrm{Pr^{3+}}}\,\mathrm{K}) [28], reflecting suppression of the electronic moment by disorder-induced splitting of the non-Kramers doublet [31]. Consistently, a.c. susceptibility measurements reveal only partial spin freezing, with χ′\chi^{\prime} remaining finite as T→0T\rightarrow 0, while neutron spectra at the lowest reported temperatures remain dominated by inelastic singlet–singlet excitations. For powder Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} in Ref. [33], neutron spectroscopy may probe an effective sample temperature (≲0.5\lesssim 0.5 K) higher than the nominal base temperature (0.020.02 K) due to thermalization limitations. A definitive determination of the ground-state behavior would therefore benefit from future measurements under well-controlled thermalization conditions that access temperatures at or below the freezing scale (∼0.25\sim 0.25 K).

By contrast, the flux-grown Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} crystals studied here exhibit experimental signatures that place them more clearly on the spin-frozen side of the phase diagram. These include a strongly reduced inelastic singlet–singlet spectral weight at base temperature, recovery of the full nuclear Schottky anomaly (∼7​J/(molPr3+​K)\sim 7\penalty\ \mathrm{J}/(\mathrm{mol}_{\mathrm{Pr^{3+}}}\,\mathrm{K})), a near-complete suppression of χ′\chi^{\prime} as T→0T\rightarrow 0, and incipient (100)(100) correlations observed in neutron scattering. Floating-zone–grown Pr2​Hf2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Hf}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [51, 50] displays several qualitatively similar trends, including subdominant inelastic singlet–singlet spectral weight [50] and a pronounced decrease of χ′\chi^{\prime} toward zero upon cooling below ∼0.1\sim 0.1 K [51], indicative of proximity to a spin-frozen regime. However, in Pr2​Hf2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Hf}_{2}\text{O}_{7} the freezing temperature appears to lie at or below the lowest experimentally accessible temperatures (≲0.075\lesssim 0.075 K) [51], and elastic neutron-scattering measurements at T=0.05T=0.05 K do not reveal clear incipient magnetic order [50]. Taken together, these observations suggest that Pr2​Hf2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Hf}_{2}\text{O}_{7} resides near the boundary of a spin-frozen regime comparable to that realized in flux-grown single-crystal Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}, with the differences most naturally attributed to a lower freezing temperature and sample-dependent disorder, rather than any qualitative distinction in the underlying physics.

More generally, these observations suggest that the diverse behavior of Pr-based pyrochlores may be understood in terms of the strength and spatial distribution of disorder-induced transverse fields arising from quenched disorder and local structural distortions. Across different compounds, the relative strength of transverse fields and magnetic interactions, parameterized by h¯/J1\bar{h}/J_{1}, appears to govern the extent to which collective spin-ice correlations survive in the presence of disorder. Within the disorder-dominated regime, the spatial distribution of transverse fields, characterized by δ​h\delta h, may further influence whether the resulting state is predominantly paramagnetic or spin-frozen. Relatively uniform transverse fields are expected to favor a singlet-dominated paramagnetic regime, whereas strongly inhomogeneous transverse fields can promote coexistence of weakly and strongly perturbed regions, leading to spin-frozen behavior.

Our Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} samples therefore realize a disorder-induced phase proximate to the ideal U⁡(1)U(1) quantum spin liquid, exhibiting coexistence of frozen and paramagnetic characteristics. This phenomenology bears similarities to Griffiths-type behavior discussed in previous theoretical work on disorder-perturbed non-Kramers pyrochlores [47, 6]. A contrasting limiting scenario is a more homogeneous frozen state, in which the average transverse field h¯\bar{h} lies just below the critical value hch_{c}. In practice, these two limits are difficult to distinguish using bulk measurements, and both are broadly consistent with the observed coexistence of elastic and inelastic magnetic scattering. Although the present measurements do not directly establish the existence of spatially rare paramagnetic regions embedded within an otherwise frozen magnetic matrix, the absence of resolvable disorder in Rietveld refinement, despite signatures of local disorder from PDF analysis, is suggestive of a Griffiths-like scenario in which sparse defects generate locally enhanced transverse fields that strongly perturb nearby Pr3+ environments. Definitive discrimination between Griffiths-type and more homogeneous disorder-induced frozen states would require local probes, such as muon spin relaxation (μ\muSR), which are sensitive to spatial variations of internal magnetic fields. More broadly, our results demonstrate how weak structural disorder can qualitatively reshape the low-temperature behavior of candidate quantum spin liquids, stabilizing frozen phases that nevertheless retain clear dynamical and spatial signatures of their proximate QSI parent state.

IV Methods

IV.1 Sample preparation

Single crystals of Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} were grown via a flux method using a 1:1.2 mass ratio of dried Na2B4O7:NaF as the flux. This mixture was combined with Pr6O11, SnO2, and SnO to yield a nominal 1:5 mass ratio of Pr2Sn2O7 to flux. The resulting mixture was thoroughly ground and loaded into a 20 mL platinum crucible with a loosely fitting platinum lid, heated to 1000∘1000^{\circ}C at 200∘200^{\circ}C/h, held for 6 h, and then cooled to 500∘500^{\circ}C at 11–1.5∘1.5^{\circ}C/h. Approximately 50% of the flux mass was lost due to volatilization. Residual flux was removed by dissolution in boiling water. The resulting crystals are well-faceted, dark-red octahedra, typically 11–2020 mg in mass and millimeter-sized.

For single-crystal neutron scattering experiments, a total of 175 well-faceted octahedral crystals were mounted on both sides of two oxygen-free copper plates using GE varnish. The crystals covered a rectangular area of approximately 1.51.5 cm (vertical) ×\times 1.01.0 cm (horizontal) on each plate, with the (H​H​L)(HHL) scattering plane oriented horizontally. The resulting assembly behaves effectively as a single crystal with a modest mosaic spread, with a total mass of approximately 1.271.27 g and an estimated mosaicity of ∼5∘\sim 5^{\circ} full width at half maximum (FWHM).

For neutron powder diffraction measurements performed on the Nanoscale-Ordered Materials Diffractometer (NOMAD), approximately 500 mg of single-crystal material was gently crushed and sealed in a 3-mm-diameter quartz capillary. The resulting fine-grained powder (or microcrystalline aggregate) exhibits a characteristic dark-red coloration. Photographs of the samples, along with diffraction measurements confirming the mosaicity, are provided in Fig. S1 of the Supplementary Materials.

IV.2 Bulk characterization

A single-crystal specimen with a mass of approximately 1 mg was used for heat capacity and a.c. susceptibility measurements using a Quantum Design 9 T Dynacool Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS), covering both the conventional 4He and dilution refrigerator (DR) temperature ranges. Additional bulk characterization, including magnetization-versus-field measurements and d.c. susceptibility data, is provided in Sec. S2 and Fig. S3 of the Supplementary Materials.

For the heat capacity data, the nuclear Schottky anomaly in CpC_{p} was analyzed using two models: (1) the analytical model of Kimura et al. [28], with μhypPr=1.9​μB\mu_{\mathrm{hyp}}^{\mathrm{Pr}}=1.9\penalty\ \mu_{\mathrm{B}} and no scaling factor; and (2) a statistical (Gopal) model [23], which treats the system as a multilevel scheme with six evenly spaced energy levels (nuclear spin I=52I=\frac{5}{2} for Pr141{}^{141}\mathrm{Pr}), with a level spacing of ϵr=0.011\epsilon_{r}=0.011 meV. Both models reproduce the broad maximum in CpC_{p} near 0.1 K. The heat capacity data and parameters obtained from model (1) closely resemble those reported for Pr2​Zr2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Zr}_{2}\text{O}_{7} sample 1 in Ref. [55].

The magnetic entropy SmS_{m} [Fig. 3(ii)] was obtained by subtracting both the nuclear contribution (modeled using the Gopal approach) and the lattice contribution (estimated from non-magnetic La2Sn2O7) from the measured CpC_{p}, and integrating the resulting magnetic contribution Cm/TC_{m}/T. Subtraction using either the Kimura or Gopal model yields essentially identical results for the magnetic entropy. We note that a definitive separation between nuclear Schottky and electronic magnetic contributions to the heat capacity is not possible. Consequently, the fitted nuclear Schottky peak may be slightly overestimated, with a corresponding excess in the measured heat capacity arising from electronic magnetic contributions. The magnetic entropy shown in Fig. 3(ii) should therefore be regarded as an approximate lower-bound estimate. In particular, the entropy recovered between the base temperature (∼0.1\sim 0.1 K) and 10 K may be somewhat larger than the value close to R⁡(ln⁡2−12​ln⁡32)R\!\left(\ln 2-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\tfrac{3}{2}\right) obtained from the present subtraction procedure.

To extract the “slow” timescale of spin dynamics [56] from the real part χ′\chi^{\prime} of the a.c. susceptibility, we employ a damped harmonic oscillator model [57, 33]:

χ′​(f)=χS+χT−χS1+(2​π​f​τ)2,\chi^{\prime}(f)=\chi_{S}+\frac{\chi_{T}-\chi_{S}}{1+(2\pi f\tau)^{2}}, (3)

where ff is the driving frequency, τ\tau is the characteristic spin correlation time, χS\chi_{S} is the adiabatic (high-frequency) susceptibility, and χT\chi_{T} is the isothermal (low-frequency) susceptibility. Details of the fits at each temperature are provided in Fig. S2 of the Supplementary Materials.

IV.3 Single-crystal neutron scattering experiment

Magnetic diffuse scattering measurements were performed on the Wide-Angle Neutron Diffractometer (WAND2) at the High Flux Isotope Reactor (HFIR), Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), using unpolarized neutrons with an incident wavelength λ=1.5​Å\lambda=1.5\penalty\ \text{\AA}. Two primary data sets were collected at T=0.3T=0.3 K and T=1T=1 K. Background subtraction was performed using high-temperature measurements at T=10T=10 K and T=20T=20 K, respectively. The use of two background data sets compensates for a minor change in background conditions during the experiment. As indicated by the heat-capacity analysis, most spin-ice entropy is released below 10 K (see Fig. 3ii). Spin-ice correlations are therefore expected to be largely absent for T≥10T\geq 10 K, and the magnetic structure factor should consequently exhibit only weak 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence (∝|F⁡(Q)|2\propto|F(Q)|^{2}, where F⁡(Q)F(Q) is the magnetic form factor of Pr3+), making the T≥10T\geq 10 K data an appropriate reference for removing the nuclear background and isolating the 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence of the magnetic scattering. Inelastic neutron scattering measurements were carried out on the Cold Neutron Chopper Spectrometer (CNCS) at the Spallation Neutron Source (SNS), ORNL. Data were collected at T=0.05T=0.05 K, 0.50.5 K, and 1010 K using incident neutron energies of 0.990.99 and 3.323.32 meV. High-flux chopper configurations were employed to optimize energy resolution and reciprocal-space coverage, yielding elastic energy resolutions (FWHM) of approximately 0.020.02 and 0.10.1 meV, respectively.

The data shown in Fig. 4a–c were processed to remove a weak background feature present at all temperatures; details are provided in Sec. S4.2 (see also Figs. S6 and S7) of the Supplementary Materials. For the slices in Fig. 4d–j, data collected at T=10T=10 K were subtracted to isolate the magnetic scattering, following the same rationale as for the WAND2 data. For the constant-energy slices shown in Fig. 4d–j, the color scale of each panel is centered on its mean intensity after subtraction of the corresponding T=10T=10 K background. For a given energy range, the color-scale span is chosen to be identical for the T=0.05T=0.05 K and T=0.5T=0.5 K datasets. Consequently, these plots are designed to facilitate comparison of the momentum dependence of the scattering between temperatures within each energy transfer, rather than quantitative comparison of absolute intensities across different energy transfers. The energy integration windows were chosen to avoid leakage from the elastic line; the corresponding resolution analysis is presented in Sec. S4.3 (see also Fig. S10). Energy-gain and energy-loss channels were combined to improve statistical accuracy and to account for temperature-dependent background variations and possible non-equilibrium effects associated with spin freezing. More details and the separated channels are presented in Sec. S4.4 and Fig. S11. Additional CNCS data are provided in Figs. S6, S8, and S9 of the Supplementary Materials.

For both WAND2 and CNCS measurements, the sample was rotated about the vertical [1​1¯​0][1\bar{1}0] axis over a total angular range of 180∘180^{\circ}, with step sizes of 0.1∘0.1^{\circ} and 1∘1^{\circ}, respectively. All neutron-scattering data were reduced and processed using the Mantid software suite [4].

IV.4 Mean-field model of split non-Kramers doublets

To interpret the temperature evolution of the singlet–singlet excitation, we summarize a local mean-field framework developed for disordered non-Kramers pyrochlores [31, 1]. Each Pr3+ site ii can be described by an effective two-level Hamiltonian,

ℋmf=(0−hi−hiEJ),\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{mf}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-h_{i}\\ -h_{i}&E_{J}\end{pmatrix}, (4)

expressed in the basis of pseudospin states aligned parallel (|+⟩\ket{+}) and antiparallel (|−⟩\ket{-}) to the local 𝒛^|⟨111⟩\hat{\bm{z}}\parallel\langle 111\rangle easy axis. The parameter hih_{i} is defined in Eq. 1, while EJE_{J} represents the longitudinal spin-flip energy cost associated with transitions between |+⟩\ket{+} and |−⟩\ket{-}.

Within a mean-field approximation, EJE_{J} is determined by the surrounding pseudospin configuration,

EJ=2​∑n,jJn​⟨σjz⟩,E_{J}=2\sum_{n,j}J_{n}\langle\sigma_{j}^{z}\rangle, (5)

where the sum runs over the nnth-nearest neighbors jj of site ii. Retaining only nearest-neighbor interactions J1J_{1} and assuming a local two-in–two-out configuration yields EJ=4​J1E_{J}=4J_{1}. For clarity, transverse exchange terms J±J_{\pm} and J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} in Eq. 1 are neglected. At the mean-field level, inclusion of J±J_{\pm} would primarily renormalize the effective transverse field via hi→hi+J±​∑n,j⟨σjx⟩h_{i}\rightarrow h_{i}+J_{\pm}\sum_{n,j}\langle\sigma_{j}^{x}\rangle once quadrupolar correlations develop at low temperature.

The Hamiltonian in Eq. 4 yields a split spectrum consisting of a ground state |GS⟩\ket{\mathrm{GS}} and an excited state |EX⟩\ket{\mathrm{EX}}, separated by an energy gap Δ=EJ2+4​hi2\Delta=\sqrt{E_{J}^{2}+4h_{i}^{2}}. The elastic and inelastic neutron-scattering intensities associated with transitions within the split doublet are

Iel∝|⟨GS|​σz​|GS⟩|2=EJ2Δ2,Iinel​(Δ)∝|⟨EX|​σz​|GS⟩|2=4​hi2Δ2,\displaystyle\begin{split}I_{\mathrm{el}}&\propto\left|\bra{\mathrm{GS}}\sigma^{z}\ket{\mathrm{GS}}\right|^{2}=\frac{E_{J}^{2}}{\Delta^{2}},\\ I_{\mathrm{inel}}(\Delta)&\propto\left|\bra{\mathrm{EX}}\sigma^{z}\ket{\mathrm{GS}}\right|^{2}=\frac{4h_{i}^{2}}{\Delta^{2}},\end{split} (6)

since neutrons predominantly probe the magnetic dipole moment along the local easy axis, and J^z∝σz\hat{J}^{z}\propto\sigma^{z} [37, 12] within the effective two-level subspace.

In the spin-ice limit (hi=0h_{i}=0), the pseudospins align along 𝒛^\hat{\bm{z}}. The ground state |GS⟩\ket{\mathrm{GS}} corresponds to the “two-in, two-out” configuration, while |EX⟩\ket{\mathrm{EX}} corresponds to a single spin-flip defect (i.e., the creation of a pair of spinons). In this limit, the inelastic matrix element vanishes (Iinel=0I_{\mathrm{inel}}=0), and the spectral weight resides entirely in the elastic channel. In the opposite limit (hi≫EJh_{i}\gg E_{J}), the pseudospin is rotated nearly perpendicular to the easy axis, yielding a singlet ground state |GS⟩→(|+⟩+|−⟩)/2\ket{\mathrm{GS}}\rightarrow(\ket{+}+\ket{-})/\sqrt{2}. Consequently, the elastic contribution is suppressed (Iel→0I_{\mathrm{el}}\rightarrow 0), and the spectral weight is transferred entirely to the inelastic channel at energy Δ\Delta.

At high temperatures, spin-ice correlations are negligible and the exchange field vanishes to leading order (EJ≈0E_{J}\approx 0). In this regime, the low-energy magnetic response is governed by singlet–singlet excitations with local splittings Δi=2​hi\Delta_{i}=2h_{i}, distributed according to a probability density p⁡(Δ)p(\Delta). Upon cooling below T∼1T\sim 1 K, spin-ice correlations progressively develop, generating a finite exchange field ∑n,jJn​⟨σjz⟩\sum_{n,j}J_{n}\langle\sigma_{j}^{z}\rangle (and hence EJE_{J}). Within this mean-field picture, the excitation energies shift to higher values, Δi→(2​hi)2+EJ2\Delta_{i}\rightarrow\sqrt{(2h_{i})^{2}+E_{J}^{2}}. Simultaneously, the growing exchange field favors alignment of the pseudospins along the local 𝒛^\hat{\bm{z}} axis, leading to a progressive transfer of spectral weight from the inelastic to the elastic channel for sites where hi∼EJh_{i}\sim E_{J}.

IV.5 Fitting neutron spectroscopy data

The spectra in Fig. 4a–c were analyzed using the composite fitting function

I⁡(ℏ​ω)=a0​exp⁡[−(ℏ​ω)22​σ2]+∫d​ω′​R​(ω−ω′)​S​(ω′)+C0,\begin{split}I(\hbar\omega)&=a_{0}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\hbar\omega)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right]+\int d\omega^{\prime}\,R(\omega-\omega^{\prime})\,S(\omega^{\prime})+C_{0},\end{split} (7)

where the Gaussian term accounts for elastic contributions, including nuclear scattering, static magnetic correlations, and residual instrumental background, as illustrated in Fig. 4i–iii. The Gaussian width σ≈0.0087\sigma\approx 0.0087 meV was fixed to the instrumental energy resolution. The second term represents the quasielastic and inelastic magnetic response S⁡(ω)S(\omega) convoluted with the instrumental energy resolution function,

R⁡(ω)=12​π​σ​exp⁡[−(ℏ​ω)22​σ2],R(\omega)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\hbar\omega)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right], (8)

where the same value of σ\sigma was used. The constant term C0C_{0} accounts for a small residual background.

At T=10T=10 K, where spin-ice correlations are negligible, the system can be treated as an ensemble of effectively independent doublets, each split by a local energy Δi=2​hi\Delta_{i}=2h_{i} at site ii. Starting from generalized susceptibility for a two-level system split by energy Δ\Delta, we have [31]

χ⁡(ω,Δ)=|ζ(Δ)|2tanh(Δ2​kB​T)[1ℏ​ω−Δ+i​0+−1ℏ​ω+Δ+i​0+].\begin{split}\chi(\omega,\Delta)&=|\zeta(\Delta)|^{2}\tanh\!\left(\frac{\Delta}{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\right)\left[\frac{1}{\hbar\omega-\Delta+i0^{+}}\right.\\ &\left.-\frac{1}{\hbar\omega+\Delta+i0^{+}}\right].\end{split} (9)

Here ζ⁡(Δ)=⟨EX|​σz​|GS⟩\zeta(\Delta)=\bra{\mathrm{EX}}\sigma^{z}\ket{\mathrm{GS}} is the matrix element of dipole moment operator between the ground state |GS⟩\ket{\mathrm{GS}} and the excited state |EX⟩\ket{\mathrm{EX}} of the split doublet, and we have ζ⁡(Δ)∼1\zeta(\Delta)\sim 1 at T=10T=10 K. This leads to spin-spin correlation function for a two-level system S⁡(ω,Δ)S(\omega,\Delta) through the fluctuation–dissipation theorem:

S⁡(ω,Δ)=1π​11−exp(−ℏω/kBT)​χ′′​(ω,Δ)=|ζ⁡(Δ)|2π​11−exp(−ℏω/kBT)​tanh⁡(Δ2​kB​T)×(δ⁡(ℏ​ω−Δ)−δ⁡(ℏ​ω+Δ))\begin{split}S(\omega,\Delta)&=\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{1}{1-\exp(-\hbar\omega/k_{\mathrm{B}}T)}\chi^{\prime\prime}(\omega,\Delta)\\ &=\frac{|\zeta(\Delta)|^{2}}{\pi}\frac{1}{1-\exp(-\hbar\omega/k_{\mathrm{B}}T)}\tanh\!\left(\frac{\Delta}{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\right)\\ &\times\left(\delta(\hbar\omega-\Delta)-\delta(\hbar\omega+\Delta)\right)\end{split} (10)

Following Ref. [58], we model the effects of quenched disorder by assuming a half-Lorentzian distribution of the transverse field hih_{i},

p⁡(h)=2π​Γhh2+Γh2,h≥0,p(h)=\frac{2}{\pi}\frac{\Gamma_{h}}{h^{2}+\Gamma_{h}^{2}},\qquad h\geq 0, (11)

with p⁡(h)=0p(h)=0 for h<0h<0. This gives a distribution of local split energy Δ\Delta,

p⁡(Δ)=2π​2​ΓhΔ2+(2​Γh)2,Δ≥0,p(\Delta)=\frac{2}{\pi}\frac{2\Gamma_{h}}{\Delta^{2}+(2\Gamma_{h})^{2}},\qquad\Delta\geq 0, (12)

with p⁡(Δ)=0p(\Delta)=0 for Δ<0\Delta<0. The dynamical correlation function averaged over this distribution is then given by

S⁡(ω)=∫0∞d​Δ​p​(Δ)​S​(ω,Δ)=C​tanh⁡(ℏ​ω2​kB​T)1−exp(−ℏω/kBT)​2​Γh(ℏ​ω)2+(2​Γh)2=C1+exp(−ℏω/kBT)​2​Γh(ℏ​ω)2+(2​Γh)2,\begin{split}S(\omega)&=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}\Delta\,p(\Delta)\,S(\omega,\Delta)\\ &=C\,\frac{\tanh\!\left(\frac{\hbar\omega}{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\right)}{1-\exp(-\hbar\omega/ k_{\mathrm{B}} T)}\frac{2\Gamma_{h}}{(\hbar\omega)^{2}+(2\Gamma_{h})^{2}}\\ &=\frac{C}{1+\exp(-\hbar\omega/ k_{\mathrm{B}} T)}\frac{2\Gamma_{h}}{(\hbar\omega)^{2}+(2\Gamma_{h})^{2}},\end{split} (13)

where CC is an overall intensity scale factor. This expression is used to fit the spectra at T=10T=10 K [Fig. 4c], yielding Γh=0.063​(3)\Gamma_{h}=0.063(3) meV. For comparison with lower temperatures, the total magnetic scattering intensity I0I_{0} is defined by integrating Eq. 13 over ℏ​ω∈[−0.6, 0.6]\hbar\omega\in[-0.6,\,0.6] meV.

To phenomenologically describe the inelastic response below T∼1T\sim 1 K, we adopt a damped harmonic oscillator (DHO) form [36],

S⁡(ω)=C1​ℏ​ω1−exp(−ℏω/kBT)​1[(ℏ​ω)2−f2]2+(ℏ​ω​z)2,\begin{split}S(\omega)&=C_{1}\frac{\hbar\omega}{1-\exp(-\hbar\omega/ k_{\mathrm{B}} T)}\frac{1}{\left[(\hbar\omega)^{2}-f^{2}\right]^{2}+(\hbar\omega z)^{2}},\end{split} (14)

where ff denotes the characteristic mode frequency and zz is the damping parameter, both expressed in energy units. C1C_{1} is an overall intensity scale factor.

At T=0.05T=0.05 K [Fig.4a], fitting the spectra with Eq. 14 yields f=0.26​(1)f=0.26(1) meV and z=0.24​(3)z=0.24(3) meV, corresponding to the underdamped regime (f>z/2f>z/2) [30]. In this limit, the response is well approximated by a double-Lorentzian form,

S⁡(ω)∼C11−exp(−ℏω/kBT)×[Γ(ℏ​ω−Egap)2+Γ2−Γ(ℏ​ω+Egap)2+Γ2],\begin{split}S(\omega)&\sim\frac{C_{1}}{1-\exp(-\hbar\omega/ k_{\mathrm{B}} T)}\\ &\quad\times\left[\frac{\Gamma}{(\hbar\omega-E_{\mathrm{gap}})^{2}+\Gamma^{2}}-\frac{\Gamma}{(\hbar\omega+E_{\mathrm{gap}})^{2}+\Gamma^{2}}\right],\end{split} (15)

with Egap=f2−z2/4=0.23​(1)E_{\mathrm{gap}}=\sqrt{f^{2}-z^{2}/4}=0.23(1) meV and Γ=z/2=0.12​(2)\Gamma=z/2=0.12(2) meV. The linewidth (Γ\Gamma) is comparable to ΓΔ=2​Γh=0.13​(1)\Gamma_{\Delta}=2\Gamma_{h}=0.13(1) meV obtained at T=10T=10 K, indicating that it is primarily governed by the distribution of quenched disorder. Integration over ℏ​ω∈[−0.6, 0.6]\hbar\omega\in[-0.6,\,0.6] meV shows that the gapped excitation accounts for approximately 30%30\% of I0I_{0}.

At T=0.5T=0.5 K [Fig.4b], fitting the spectra with Eq. 14 yields f=0.17​(1)f=0.17(1) meV and z=0.39​(3)z=0.39(3) meV, placing the system in the overdamped regime (f<z/2f<z/2) [30]. The response can then be interpreted as two overdamped relaxational modes with damping rates (expressed in energy units) Γ1,2=z/2±z2/4−f2=0.29​(5)\Gamma_{1,2}=z/2\pm\sqrt{z^{2}/4-f^{2}}=0.29(5) meV and 0.10​(2)0.10(2) meV, corresponding to timescales τ1,2=ℏ/Γ1,2=2.3​(4)\tau_{1,2}=\hbar/\Gamma_{1,2}=2.3(4) ps and 6.6​(1.6)6.6(1.6) ps. Integrating Eq. 14 over the energy range ℏ​ω∈[−0.6, 0.6]\hbar\omega\in[-0.6,\,0.6] meV shows that the low-energy dynamical response, which is predominantly quasielastic within the present energy resolution, accounts for approximately 80%80\% of I0I_{0}. We note that such quasielastic spectral weight may arise either from intrinsic relaxational dynamics or from unresolved low-energy inelastic excitations, such as photon-like modes expected in a QSI regime.

IV.6 Powder neutron refinement

Powder neutron-diffraction data were collected from pulverized single-crystal specimens at T=100T=100 K and T=300T=300 K. Rietveld refinements of the diffraction patterns were carried out using the software package TOPAS [13]. Neutron pair distribution function (PDF) analysis was performed using the PDFgui [16] software package. For PDF analysis, a stoichiometric structural model was refined over short real-space distances up to 10 Å.

Uncertainty estimation.

Unless otherwise stated, uncertainties of data points in all figures correspond to one standard deviation (1σ\sigma) statistical errors. For parameters obtained from least-squares or χ2\chi^{2} minimization procedures in diffuse-scattering fits, uncertainties were determined from the parameter range satisfying χ2<χmin2​(1+1N−M)\chi^{2}<\chi^{2}_{\min}\left(1+\frac{1}{N-M}\right), where NN is the number of data points and MM is the number of fitted parameters, taking into account the numerical resolution of the parameter grid. For all other fitted quantities, uncertainties were estimated from covariance-matrix analysis near the best-fit solution. Systematic uncertainties are not included.

Supplementary Materials for “Disorder-induced proximate quantum spin ice phase in Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}”

S1 Supplementary Figures and Tables

Unless otherwise stated, uncertainties of data points in all figures correspond to one standard deviation (1σ\sigma) statistical errors. For parameters obtained from χ2\chi^{2} minimization of the diffuse-scattering fits, uncertainties were determined from the parameter range satisfying χ2<χmin2​(1+1N−M)\chi^{2}<\chi^{2}_{\min}\left(1+\frac{1}{N-M}\right), where NN is the number of data points and MM is the number of fitted parameters, taking into account the numerical resolution of the parameter grid. For all other fitted quantities obtained from least-squares fitting procedures, uncertainties were estimated from covariance-matrix analysis near the best-fit solution. Systematic uncertainties are not included.

S2 Supplementary bulk characterization of Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}

Magnetization versus field measurements at T=2T=2 K on single-crystal Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7} samples with masses of approximately 5 mg are shown in Fig. S3c. The induced magnetic moments MM at the maximum applied field μ0​H=7\mu_{0}H=7 T are measured to be 1.64​μB/Pr3+1.64\penalty\ \mu_{\mathrm{B}}/\mathrm{Pr^{3+}}, 1.33​μB/Pr3+1.33\penalty\ \mu_{\mathrm{B}}/\mathrm{Pr^{3+}}, and 1.19​μB/Pr3+1.19\penalty\ \mu_{\mathrm{B}}/\mathrm{Pr^{3+}} for fields applied along the [100][100], [111][111], and [110][110] directions, respectively. For comparison, the expected saturated moments in a pyrochlore lattice with Ising anisotropy along the local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle directions and effective ferromagnetic (FM) coupling between nearest neighbors are gJ​J/3g_{J}J/\sqrt{3} for the [100][100] direction, gJ​J/2g_{J}J/2 for [111][111], and gJ​J/6g_{J}J/\sqrt{6} for [110][110] [18]. Both the observed ordering of the induced moments (from largest to smallest) and their relative ratios are consistent with the predictions for a magnetic pyrochlore with nearest neighbor FM coupling and easy-axis anisotropy. Quantitative deviations may arise from slight misalignments during sample mounting, mass uncertainty due to residual impurity phases, or the fact that full saturation may not have been achieved at μ0​H=7\mu_{0}H=7 T. The temperature dependence of the d.c. magnetic susceptibility was measured with the magnetic field applied along the [100][100], [111][111], and [110][110] crystallographic directions using the same single-crystal samples. To obtain a representative bulk behavior, we compute a powder-averaged d.c. susceptibility for a cubic system using the expression χpowderDC=(3​χ100DC+6​χ110DC+4​χ111DC)/13\chi_{\mathrm{powder}}^{\mathrm{DC}}=(3\chi_{100}^{\mathrm{DC}}+6\chi_{110}^{\mathrm{DC}}+4\chi_{111}^{\mathrm{DC}})/13 [8], and plot the results in Fig. S3d,e. This powder-averaged d.c. susceptibility is also used to normalize the real part of the a.c. susceptibility χ′\chi^{\prime} presented in Fig. 3a of the main text. A Curie–Weiss fit to the high-temperature regime yields a Curie–Weiss temperature of θCW=−0.23​(2)\theta_{\mathrm{CW}}=-0.23(2) K and an effective moment of μeff=2.78​(1)​μB/Pr3+\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}=2.78(1)\penalty\ \mu_{\mathrm{B}}/\mathrm{Pr^{3+}}, in good agreement with the powder measurements reported in Ref. [33].

S3 Modeling of magnetic diffuse-scattering data

To model the magnetic diffuse scattering observed in single-crystal Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}, we use the SPINTERACT software suite [34]. For quantum and classical models, we write the Hamiltonian in terms of unit Pauli matrices or unit-length Ising variables, respectively, corresponding to an effective spin-1/21/2 on each Pr3+ site with an effective gg-factor g∥=5.17g_{\parallel}=5.17 along the local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle direction [40]. The local coordinate frames (𝐚^i,𝐛^i,𝐞^i)(\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{i},\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i},\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{i}) are defined as in Ref. [44]:

𝐞^0=13(1,1,1),𝐚^0=16(−2,1,1),𝐞^1=13(1,−1,−1),𝐚^1=16(−2,−1,−1),𝐞^2=13(−1,1,−1),𝐚^2=16(2,1,−1),𝐞^3=13(−1,−1,1),𝐚^3=16(2,−1,1),\displaystyle\begin{split}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{0}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(1,1,1),\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \hat{\mathbf{a}}_{0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(-2,1,1),\\ \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{1}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(1,-1,-1),\quad\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(-2,-1,-1),\\ \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{2}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-1,1,-1),\quad\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2,1,-1),\\ \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{3}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-1,-1,1),\quad\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2,-1,1),\end{split} (S1)

corresponding to the four Pr3+ ions located at 𝐫^0=(0.5,0.5,0.5)\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{0}=(0.5,0.5,0.5), 𝐫^1=(0.5,0.75,0.75)\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{1}=(0.5,0.75,0.75), 𝐫^2=(0.75,0.5,0.75)\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{2}=(0.75,0.5,0.75), and 𝐫^3=(0.75,0.75,0.5)\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{3}=(0.75,0.75,0.5) in the face-centered cubic unit cell, with 𝐛^i=𝐞^i×𝐚^i\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i}=\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{i}\times\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{i}. A magnetic background following the form factor |F⁡(Q)|2|F(Q)|^{2} for Pr3+ is subtracted to simulate the experimental high-temperature background removal. The SPINTERACT program minimizes the goodness-of-fit metric χ2\chi^{2}, defined as

χ2=∑dWd​∑i∈d(Iidata−sd​Iicalcσi)2,sd=∑iIidata​Iicalc/σi2∑i(Iicalc)2/σi2,\begin{split}\chi^{2}&=\sum_{d}W_{d}\sum_{i\in d}\left(\frac{I_{i}^{\text{data}}-s_{d}I_{i}^{\text{calc}}}{\sigma_{i}}\right)^{2},\\ s_{d}&=\frac{\sum_{i}I_{i}^{\text{data}}I_{i}^{\text{calc}}/\sigma_{i}^{2}}{\sum_{i}(I_{i}^{\text{calc}})^{2}/\sigma_{i}^{2}},\end{split} (S2)

where dd indexes a particular dataset with weight WdW_{d}, IidataI_{i}^{\text{data}} and IicalcI_{i}^{\text{calc}} denote the measured and calculated intensities for the ii-th data point, respectively, and σi\sigma_{i} is the corresponding experimental uncertainty. The scale factor sds_{d} for each dataset is determined via the linear least-squares expression given above. Throughout this work, the χ2\chi^{2} values reported in Fig. S3(a,b) correspond to the reduced goodness-of-fit metric, obtained by dividing the χ2\chi^{2} quantity defined above in Eq. S2 by the number of residual degrees of freedom (N−M)(N-M), consistent with the uncertainty criterion described at the beginning of Sec. S1.

For the quantum model, we adopt the theoretical results of Ref. [5], where the goodness-of-fit χ2\chi^{2} is plotted against the ring-exchange parameter gg [Fig. S3a] in the effective Hamiltonian:

ℋring=−∑⎔g(σi+σj−σk+σl−σm+σn−+H.c.).\mathcal{H}_{\text{ring}}=-\sum_{\hexagon}g\left(\sigma^{+}_{i}\sigma^{-}_{j}\sigma^{+}_{k}\sigma^{-}_{l}\sigma^{+}_{m}\sigma^{-}_{n}+\text{H.c.}\right). (S3)

Here, μ\mu is a theoretical tuning parameter, with μ/g=0\mu/g=0 corresponding to the quantum spin ice (QSI) limit and μ/g=1\mu/g=1 to the classical limit. This model assumes perturbative interactions with nearest-neighbor exchange J1→∞J_{1}\rightarrow\infty. Best-fit analysis yields g=0.075​(4)g=0.075(4) K≃0.0065​(3)\simeq 0.0065(3) meV in the QSI limit (μ/g=0\mu/g=0, see Fig. 2b,f in the main text). In the classical limit (μ/g=1\mu/g=1), the scattering profile is independent of gg, and the result corresponds to the J1J_{1}-only classical nearest-neighbor spin-ice (NNSI) scenario shown in Fig. 2c,g in the main text. The decreasing trend of χ2\chi^{2} with increasing gg in this regime is attributed to numerical artifacts.

For the classical dipolar spin-ice (DSI) model, we employ Onsager reaction-field theory, incorporating long-range dipolar interactions Ddip=μ0​μB2/(4​π​kB​|𝐫n​n|3)≈0.012D_{\mathrm{dip}}=\mu_{0}\mu_{\mathrm{B}}^{2}/(4\pi k_{\mathrm{B}}|\mathbf{r}_{nn}|^{3})\approx 0.012 K≃0.0010\simeq 0.0010 meV, following the convention of Ref. [34]. The total interaction JnJ_{n} between nn-th neighbor σiz\sigma_{i}^{z} terms in Eq. 1 in the main text thus includes both dipolar and exchange contributions,

Jn=Dn+Jnex.J_{n}=D_{n}+J_{n}^{\mathrm{ex}}. (S4)

Further-neighbor interactions, in particular J2J_{2} and J3J_{3}, have also been invoked to explain the magnetic correlations observed below the spin-freezing transition in Dy2​Ti2​O7\text{Dy}_{2}\text{Ti}_{2}\text{O}_{7} [61, 45]. The Hamiltonian, including exchange interactions up to next-nearest neighbors (J2J_{2}) and neglecting disorder terms, is given by

ℋ=∑⟨i​j⟩1(J1ex+D1)​σiz​σjz+∑⟨i​j⟩2(J2ex+D2)​σiz​σjz+further-neighbor dipolar terms,\begin{split}\mathcal{H}&=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{1}}(J_{1}^{\mathrm{ex}}+D_{1})\,\sigma_{i}^{z}\sigma_{j}^{z}+\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{2}}(J_{2}^{\mathrm{ex}}+D_{2})\,\sigma_{i}^{z}\sigma_{j}^{z}\\ &\quad+\text{further-neighbor dipolar terms},\end{split} (S5)

where D1=53​(g∥​S)2​Ddip=0.13D_{1}=\frac{5}{3}(g_{\parallel}S)^{2}D_{\mathrm{dip}}=0.13 K ≃0.011\simeq 0.011 meV (S=1/2S=1/2) [14] is the effective nearest-neighbor dipolar coupling. The next-nearest-neighbor dipolar coupling follows from the corresponding local-axis geometry as D2=−D1/(53)=−0.015D_{2}=-D_{1}/(5\sqrt{3})=-0.015 K ≃−0.0013\simeq-0.0013 meV. All parameters are expressed in the local coordinate frames defined in Eq. S1 and the long-ranged nature of the dipolar interaction was implemented using Ewald summation. The magnetic diffuse scattering pattern alone does not effectively constrain the magnitude of J1exJ_{1}^{\mathrm{ex}}, so we complement the fitting with powder-averaged d.c. susceptibility data (Wd=1W_{d}=1 for all data sets). A χ2\chi^{2} map of the fits to the magnetic diffuse scattering and d.c. susceptibility data as a function of J1exJ_{1}^{\mathrm{ex}} and J2exJ_{2}^{\mathrm{ex}} is shown in Fig. S3b, with the optimal parameters found to be J1ex=0.25​(3)J_{1}^{\mathrm{ex}}=0.25(3) K≃0.0215​(26)\simeq 0.0215(26) meV and J2ex=−0.018​(1)J_{2}^{\mathrm{ex}}=-0.018(1) K≃−0.0016​(1)\simeq-0.0016(1) meV. We estimate an effective nearest-neighbor interaction of J1=J1ex+D1≈0.033J_{1}=J_{1}^{\mathrm{ex}}+D_{1}\approx 0.033 meV, which is used in the Discussion section of the main text. The corresponding fits to the susceptibility data are shown in Fig. S3d,e.

The sign convention for the fitted interaction parameters is illustrated in Fig. S4. An antiferromagnetic nearest-neighbor interaction J1=J1ex+D1>0J_{1}=J_{1}^{\mathrm{ex}}+D_{1}>0 between pseudo-spins in the local frame favors the canonical “two-in, two-out” spin configuration on each tetrahedron. In contrast, a ferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor interaction J2=J2ex+D2<0J_{2}=J_{2}^{\mathrm{ex}}+D_{2}<0 in the local frame favors a “loop” structure, where spins on three next-nearest-neighbor sites around a hexagonal plaquette align either all clockwise or all counterclockwise relative to the plaquette center.

We note that a model including only J1exJ_{1}^{\mathrm{ex}} and dipolar interactions fails to reproduce the observed 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence at T=0.3T=0.3 K (see Fig. S5a,b). Incorporating a finite next-nearest-neighbor exchange J2exJ_{2}^{\mathrm{ex}} is necessary to capture the 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence [Fig. S5c].

S4 Supplementary neutron spectroscopy analysis

In this section, we present supplementary neutron spectroscopy data and associated analysis for single-crystal Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}. These include additional figures as well as technical aspects of data processing, including background subtraction, energy resolution considerations, and the treatment of energy-gain and energy-loss channels.

S4.1 Supplementary neutron spectral data

Figure S6 shows the powder-averaged scattering intensity as a function of energy transfer ℏ​ω\hbar\omega. For measurements with Ei=0.99E_{i}=0.99 meV, a gapped inelastic continuum centered at ℏ​ω≈0.2\hbar\omega\approx 0.2 meV is observed at T=0.05T=0.05 K, while a broad low-energy continuum extending up to ℏ​ω≈0.6\hbar\omega\approx 0.6 meV is observed at T=0.5T=0.5 K [Fig. S6a,c,d]. In contrast, the Ei=3.32E_{i}=3.32 meV data show no additional inelastic features above ∼0.6\sim 0.6 meV [Fig. S6f,g]. Figure S8 presents false-color maps of the scattering intensity as functions of momentum transfer along the [00​L][00L] and [H​H​H][HHH] directions and energy transfer, measured with Ei=0.99E_{i}=0.99 meV. These maps exhibit spectral features consistent with those observed in the powder-averaged data [Fig. S6].

S4.2 Removal of background feature

In the raw data shown in Fig. S6a, we identify a temperature-independent, shoulder-like background feature centered near ℏ​ω∼0.1\hbar\omega\sim 0.1 meV. This feature is absent on the energy-gain side (ℏ​ω<0\hbar\omega<0) at T=10T=10 K. To remove this contribution, we assume that the background is temperature independent and that the energy-gain side contains negligible background. This assumption is supported by the absence of significant intensity for Q>0.2Q>0.2 Å-1 at ℏ​ω<0\hbar\omega<0 and T=0.05T=0.05 K (Fig. S6c), where true inelastic scattering is expected to be strongly suppressed.

As illustrated in Fig. S7a, we use the energy-gain-side data at T=10T=10 K to calculate the corresponding energy-loss spectrum (ℏ​ω>0\hbar\omega>0) via the detailed balance relation I⁡(|ℏ​ω|)=I⁡(−|ℏ​ω|)​exp⁡(|ℏ​ω|/kB​T)I(|\hbar\omega|)=I(-|\hbar\omega|)\exp(|\hbar\omega|/k_{\mathrm{B}} T) (red curve). The asymmetry in energy resolution between the energy-gain and energy-loss sides is neglected, as the relevant energy range lies close to the elastic line. The background contribution (green curve) is then obtained by subtracting the calculated energy-loss spectrum (red) from the measured data (black). This estimated background is subtracted from the spectra at all three temperatures, yielding the corrected data shown in Fig. S7b, which are used for the quantitative analysis in Fig. 3a,b,c of the main text.

S4.3 Energy resolution and elastic leakage analysis

In Fig. S9a–h, we present constant-energy 𝑸\bm{Q} maps analogous to those shown in Fig. 4d–j, but measured with an incident energy of Ei=0.99E_{i}=0.99 meV. This configuration provides superior energy resolution, albeit at the expense of reduced neutron flux and more limited 𝑸\bm{Q} coverage. At T=0.05T=0.05 K, signatures of incipient (100) correlations are observed as diffuse scattering centered near the (001)(001) and (110)(110) positions (Fig. S9b). However, owing to limited statistics and restricted 𝑸\bm{Q} range, the momentum dependence of the low-energy (quasielastic and inelastic) response at T=0.5T=0.5 K, as well as the gapped inelastic features at T=0.05T=0.05 K, cannot be clearly resolved in this configuration.

To overcome these limitations, we employed the Ei=3.32E_{i}=3.32 meV configuration, which provides broader 𝑸\bm{Q} coverage and higher neutron flux. This enables resolution of the 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence of the gapped excitation centered at ℏ​ω=0.23​(1)\hbar\omega=0.23(1) meV at T=0.05T=0.05 K. Figure S10a shows the powder-averaged scattering intensity as a function of energy transfer ℏ​ω\hbar\omega at T=0.05T=0.05 K, measured near the horizontal (H​H​L)(HHL) plane (K≤0.15K\leq 0.15 rlu along [K​K¯​0][K\bar{K}0]). Also shown is the intensity integrated within ±0.15\pm 0.15 rlu around the (111) Bragg peak, scaled to match the elastic peak in Fig. S10i. The energy profile of the (111) peak provides an in-situ measure of the instrumental energy resolution, with approximately 99.49%99.49\% of the total intensity confined within ℏ​ω∈[−0.2, 0.2]\hbar\omega\in[-0.2,\,0.2] meV and only ∼0.51%\sim 0.51\% outside this range.

In Fig. S10b, we present the 𝑸\bm{Q} map integrated over ℏ​ω∈[−0.2, 0.2]\hbar\omega\in[-0.2,\,0.2] meV, scaled by ∼0.51%\sim 0.51\% to estimate the expected elastic leakage into the [0.2, 0.6][0.2,\,0.6] meV window due to finite energy resolution. Comparison with the 𝑸\bm{Q} map integrated over |ℏ​ω|∈[0.2, 0.6]|\hbar\omega|\in[0.2,\,0.6] meV [Fig. S10c] shows that the observed “star-fish-like” 𝑸\bm{Q} dependence in this energy range cannot be attributed to elastic leakage. This conclusion is supported by both the distinct momentum-space pattern—clearly different from the elastic (100)(100)-type diffuse scattering—and the negligible magnitude of the estimated leakage relative to the measured signal.

For completeness, Figs. S9i,j show an analogous comparison for the Ei=0.99E_{i}=0.99 meV configuration between the in-plane (K≤0.1K\leq 0.1 rlu along [K​K¯​0][K\bar{K}0]) powder-averaged intensity and the (111) Bragg-peak profile integrated within ±0.1\pm 0.1 rlu and scaled to match the elastic peak. This comparison further demonstrates that the gapped excitation at ℏ​ω=0.23​(1)\hbar\omega=0.23(1) meV is well separated from the elastic line under this configuration.

S4.4 Energy-gain and energy-loss channels

In Fig. 4d–j of the main text, we present constant-energy 𝑸\bm{Q} maps at T=0.5T=0.5 K and T=0.05T=0.05 K, measured with Ei=3.32E_{i}=3.32 meV, in which the energy-gain and energy-loss contributions are combined. We do not restrict the analysis to the energy-loss side (ℏ​ω>0\hbar\omega>0) with application of the correction factor (1+exp(−ℏω/kBT))(1+\exp(-\hbar\omega/ k_{\mathrm{B}} T)), as it is unclear whether the detailed balance relation, I⁡(−|ℏ​ω|,−𝑸)=exp(−ℏω/kBT)​I​(|ℏ​ω|,𝑸)I(-|\hbar\omega|,-\bm{Q})=\exp(-\hbar\omega/ k_{\mathrm{B}} T)\,I(|\hbar\omega|,\bm{Q}), remains valid in the spin-frozen phase at T=0.05T=0.05 K.

To provide additional information, Fig. S11 shows constant-energy 𝑸\bm{Q} maps measured with Ei=3.32E_{i}=3.32 meV, with the energy-gain and energy-loss channels displayed separately. In the positive energy-transfer range ℏ​ω∈[0.2, 0.6]\hbar\omega\in[0.2,\,0.6] meV [Fig. S11c,d], the characteristic “star-fish-like” magnetic scattering exhibits stronger intensity along the [111][111] direction compared to the [001][001] direction. In contrast, in the corresponding negative energy-transfer range ℏ​ω∈[−0.6,−0.2]\hbar\omega\in[-0.6,\,-0.2] meV [Fig. S11i,j], the intensity is enhanced along the [001][001] direction.

The origin of this asymmetry is not yet clear. It may reflect non-equilibrium spin dynamics at low temperatures in Pr2​Sn2​O7\text{Pr}_{2}\text{Sn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}, or arise from experimental factors such as imperfect background subtraction or anisotropic absorption associated with the plate-like sample geometry. Further investigation will be required to distinguish between these possibilities.
